Issued at 130 AM CDT Mon Sep 7 2026

For today through Tuesday morning, there will be 3 different 
causes of showers and storm chances from different forcings moving 
through. There is a Marginal risk (level 1 of 5) for the storms 
today to become severe, with slightly different hazards from the 
different causes. For the first cause, an upper-level shortwave 
moving along the upper-level ridge that continues to sit over SD 
will help to provide upper-level support for scattered showers and 
storms early this morning into the afternoon. Similar to the 
previous mornings, a low level jet will be providing the main 
support for development as it develops over warm air and moisture 
advecting into central SD early in the morning, which then shifts 
over northeastern SD and west central MN later in the morning and 
into the afternoon. CAPE values during the morning are forecast to 
be between 1000-2000 J/kg, which will help with the development of 
elevated clusters of showers and storms in the weakly forced 
environment. Lapse rates between 5-7 C/km as well as bulk shear 
values between 30-45kts in the environment could help the storms to 
become severe. With the elevated nature to the storms, hail up 
around 1 inch and wind gusts of 60 mph will be possible. 

Along the western edge of the moisture advection, there looks to be 
a weak dry line/outflow that might develop during the afternoon into 
the evening, which will be the second cause of convection 
developing. This boundary looks to mainly move through southeastern 
parts of SD, though portions of south central SD east of the 
Missouri River and east central SD could be clipped by it. With a 
strong pressure gradient over eastern SD helping to support the low 
level jet sticking around into the afternoon hours as well as 
stronger lapse rates helping to get those winds to the surface, 
surface winds will be able to gust up around 30-40 mph over areas 
east of the Missouri River. This will help to create a fair bit of 
low level shear during the afternoon. While the weakly forced 
showers and storms talked about will be elevated in nature and not 
able to access this shear, the weak dryline/outflow moving through 
in the afternoon and evening will be able to. Because of this, the 
development of a tornado or two cannot be ruled out in these storm 
after around 1 pm CDT over southeastern and east central SD. The 
shear will also help the storms develop hail up around 1 inch and 
wind gusts of 60 mph.

An upper-level trough will be pushing the upper-level ridge out of 
SD Monday evening and overnight while also supporting a cold front 
at the surface moving through Monday afternoon overnight into 
Tuesday morning. This cold front will be the third cause of 
convection that could produce showers and storms. While models vary 
the timing of the front, it is forecast to move into central SD late 
Monday afternoon/early evening and then move through northeastern SD 
late evening overnight into Tuesday morning. The other causes of 
convection will have used up a lot of the instability over southern 
and northeastern SD through the day which will help to keep showers 
and storms from developing when the front moves through those areas. 
However, there will still be around 1000-2000 J/kg of CAPE over 
northern SD and ND as well as a fair bit of moisture to get some 
isolated showers and storms to develop over north central SD this 
evening and far northeastern SD and west central MN overnight. The 
environment will have weaker lapse rates while also having about 35-
50 kts of bulk shear in the atmosphere to help the storms become 
severe. Since the storms will be forming along a frontal boundary 
with a lot of shear, strong winds will be the primary hazard, with 
gust up around 60 mph possible. There could also be some smaller 
hail that develops, though it should be less than 1 inch.

After the cold front moves out Tuesday, a high pressure slips in 
over southwestern SD. This helps a stronger pressure gradient to 
develop over northern SD and ND, which will create stronger winds 
aloft that could get to the surface during the afternoon. There is a 
30-60% chance that there will be wind gusts greater than 35 mph 
Tuesday afternoon over north central SD. Additionally, with colder 
and drier air moving in behind the front, the relative humidity 
values will be lower. Right now, models are showing humidity values 
between 20-30% over areas west of the Missouri River. In areas where 
the strong winds and low humidity values overlap, there will be some 
fire weather concerns, especially with dry fuels already in those 
areas. This potential should be watched over the coming model runs 
as a Red Flag warning might be needed for portions of north central 
SD. The past few model runs have shifted the stronger winds to the 
north out of northern SD, and if they continue this trend, then a 
Red Flag warning might not be needed. With drier air moving in,
